2-maccabees-1:2:0.summary: God will “remember the covenant” of Jacob, Isaac and Abraham, matching the prayer that He “remember His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob”.
2-maccabees-1:2:0.why: Grounds the letter’s blessing in the Torah’s covenant promise.

2-maccabees-1:2:1.summary: Zechariah praises God to “remember His holy covenant, the oath He swore to Abraham”, the same covenant-remembrance language.
2-maccabees-1:2:1.why: Shows the same covenant hope carried into the Gospel.

2-maccabees-1:3:0.summary: Love God “with all your heart, and with all your soul”; a general echo of the wish for wholehearted, willing-souled devotion.

2-maccabees-1:3:1.summary: God promises to give “another heart, to fear Me always”, close to the prayer that He “give you all a heart to revere Him”.
2-maccabees-1:3:1.why: Shows the prayer echoes a prophetic promise of a new heart.

2-maccabees-1:3:2.summary: God will “give them another heart”; shares the idea of God giving a heart, but not specifically to revere Him.
2-maccabees-1:3:2.why: Related promise of divine heart renewal.

2-maccabees-1:4:0.summary: “The Lord opened her heart” to attend to Paul, matching the prayer “May He open your heart to His law”.
2-maccabees-1:4:0.why: Shows God opening hearts to receive His word.

2-maccabees-1:4:1.summary: The psalmist asks God to “uncover my eyes” to see wonders “from Thy law”, paralleling the prayer to open the heart to His law.
2-maccabees-1:4:1.why: Same prayer for divine opening to God’s law.

2-maccabees-1:5:0.summary: God will “hear from heaven, and be propitious” when His people pray, paralleling “hear your petitions, be reconciled to you”.
2-maccabees-1:5:0.why: Grounds the prayer in God’s promise at the temple.

2-maccabees-1:8:0.summary: Judas’s men find “the gates burned down” at the sanctuary, the same desecration as “they burned the gateway”.
2-maccabees-1:8:0.why: Narrative account of the events the letter recalls.

2-maccabees-1:8:1.summary: “They poured out innocent blood around the sanctuary”, the same phrase and event as the letter’s “poured out innocent blood”.

2-maccabees-1:9:0.summary: Judas establishes the altar’s dedication to be celebrated yearly from the twenty-fifth of “Chislev”, the festival the letter urges.
2-maccabees-1:9:0.why: Origin of the feast the letter commends.

2-maccabees-1:9:1.summary: “The feast of Dedication” in winter is the same Chislev festival the letter asks Egyptian Jews to observe.
2-maccabees-1:9:1.why: Shows the feast still kept in Jesus’ day.

2-maccabees-1:13:0.summary: Antiochus goes to Elymais “in Persia” for its temple wealth, a parallel account of the ruler’s ill-fated Persian venture.
2-maccabees-1:13:0.why: Compare the differing accounts of Antiochus’s end.

2-maccabees-1:18:0.summary: The altar’s dedication begins “on the twenty-fifth of the month of Chislev”, the same date as the temple’s purification here.
2-maccabees-1:18:0.why: Narrative origin of the festival being explained.

2-maccabees-1:18:1.summary: Iesous and Zorobabel rebuild “the altar” after exile; related restoration theme, but the letter credits Nehemiah.

2-maccabees-1:19:0.summary: The law that the altar’s “fire shall burn continually” explains why priests preserved “the altar’s fire” in exile.
2-maccabees-1:19:0.why: Explains the motive for hiding the sacred fire.

2-maccabees-1:19:1.summary: Fire from the Lord first consumed what was on “the altar”; background for the sacred altar fire, not its hiding.
2-maccabees-1:19:1.why: Origin of the holy altar fire.

2-maccabees-1:24:0.summary: Esdras’s prayer “Thou alone art the Lord. Thou madest heaven… the earth” matches the prayer to the Creator of all, the only King.
2-maccabees-1:24:0.why: Shows a shared form of Jewish prayer opening.

2-maccabees-1:25:0.summary: Israel is a “holy people” whom God has “chosen”, matching praise of God who chose the fathers and sanctified them.
2-maccabees-1:25:0.why: Grounds the prayer in Israel’s election.

2-maccabees-1:26:0.summary: Jacob became “the portion of the Lord”, the basis for the plea “Protect Thy portion”.

2-maccabees-1:27:1.summary: God will “gather Judah’s scattered ones” from the nations, matching the plea “Gather our scattered people together”.
2-maccabees-1:27:1.why: Prayer draws on prophetic ingathering promise.

2-maccabees-1:27:2.summary: The servant is to “gather Jacob” and “bring back Israel’s dispersion”, the ingathering the prayer requests.
2-maccabees-1:27:2.why: Prophetic hope behind the prayer for regathering.

2-maccabees-1:29:1.summary: Moses promises God will bring Israel into the land; a general restoration link, not the “plant” wording cited.
2-maccabees-1:29:1.why: Mosaic promise of return to the land.

2-maccabees-2:1:0.summary: “Jeremiah the prophet” among those taken away with the remnant; shares the person and deportation context only.

2-maccabees-2:5:0.summary: Jeremiah says “the ark of the covenant” will no longer be named or made, linking him to the ark’s disappearance.
2-maccabees-2:5:0.why: Jeremiah’s own word on the ark’s fate.

2-maccabees-2:5:1.summary: Lists “a golden incense altar and the ark of the covenant”, the same objects Jeremiah hid.

2-maccabees-2:5:2.summary: “The ark of His covenant was seen” in heaven; relates to the ark’s hidden fate only loosely.

2-maccabees-2:8:0.summary: “God’s glory” and “the cloud” on Sinai are what will appear again “as they were shown in the time of Moses”.

2-maccabees-2:8:2.summary: “The cloud filled the house” and “the Lord’s glory” at Solomon’s dedication, the precedent the verse cites.

2-maccabees-2:10:2.summary: God answers David “with fire from heaven” that consumes the whole burnt offering, the same sign recalled for Moses and Solomon.
2-maccabees-2:10:2.why: Another instance of heavenly fire on the altar.

2-maccabees-2:12:0.summary: Solomon keeps the feast seven days and dismisses the people “on the eighth day”, the eight days referenced.

2-maccabees-2:17:0.summary: “A royal priesthood and a holy nation” matches God restoring “the kingship, the priesthood and the sanctification”.
2-maccabees-2:17:0.why: Shows the covenant identity being restored.

2-maccabees-2:17:1.summary: “A royal priesthood, a holy nation” gives the same triad of kingship, priesthood and holiness.
2-maccabees-2:17:1.why: Shows the triad applied to the church.

2-maccabees-2:18:1.summary: “Gather us together from the nations” matches the hope that God will “gather us from under heaven into the holy place”.

2-maccabees-2:20:0.summary: Introduces “Antiochus Epiphanes”, the king whose wars the work will recount.

2-maccabees-2:20:1.summary: Antiochus’s son is made king and named “Eupator”, the son mentioned here.

2-maccabees-3:1:0.summary: Names “Simon son of Onias, the high priest”; same priestly family but not clearly the same Onias.
2-maccabees-3:1:0.why: Background on the Oniad high priests.

2-maccabees-3:10:1.summary: God is “Father of orphans and judge of widows… in His holy place”; general link to the widows’ and orphans’ temple deposits.
2-maccabees-3:10:1.why: God as protector of widows and orphans.

2-maccabees-3:24:0.summary: Heavenly horses and fiery chariots surround Elisha; shares only the motif of a divine manifestation.
2-maccabees-3:24:0.why: Divine forces revealed in a crisis.

2-maccabees-3:24:1.summary: A persecutor is overwhelmed by a sudden heavenly manifestation and falls, as Heliodorus’s company is struck by God’s power.
2-maccabees-3:24:1.why: Similar divine intervention against a persecutor.

2-maccabees-3:25:0.summary: A heavenly rider on a white horse wages war; shares only the heavenly-horseman image.

2-maccabees-3:25:1.summary: A man mounted on a red horse in a vision; shares only a supernatural rider.

2-maccabees-3:26:0.summary: “Two men stood beside them in white garments”, like the two splendidly clothed young men standing on either side of Heliodorus.
2-maccabees-3:26:0.why: Distinctive pair of radiant heavenly figures.

2-maccabees-3:26:1.summary: “Two men stood beside them in flashing clothing” matches two young men “splendid in clothing” standing beside Heliodorus.
2-maccabees-3:26:1.why: Same image of two glorious angelic men.

2-maccabees-3:27:0.summary: Saul “fell to the ground” at the divine encounter, as Heliodorus “suddenly fell to the ground”.
2-maccabees-3:27:0.why: Persecutor struck down by divine power.

2-maccabees-3:27:1.summary: Saul cannot see and is led away by others, as Heliodorus is enveloped in darkness and carried off.
2-maccabees-3:27:1.why: Same pattern of blinded, helpless persecutor.

2-maccabees-3:31:0.summary: Righteous Job is to pray for those who offended, as Onias is asked to intercede for the stricken Heliodorus.

2-maccabees-3:35:saints-20261024-2e4805b.summary: The sailors “offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made vows”, the same response as Heliodorus after deliverance.
2-maccabees-3:35:saints-20261024-2e4805b.why: Gentiles honoring Israel’s God after rescue.

2-maccabees-3:39:0.summary: The One “guarding Israel” never sleeps; general divine-guardian theme.

2-maccabees-3:39:1.summary: Solomon asks that God’s eyes be open toward “this house”; general link to God overseeing the temple.

2-maccabees-4:7:1.summary: Recalls “Jason and those with him” who revolted from the holy land, the same Jason who seized the priesthood.
2-maccabees-4:7:1.why: Identifies Jason’s role in the crisis.

2-maccabees-4:7:2.summary: Lawless men urge a covenant with the nations; related Hellenizing context, not Jason’s priestly fraud.

2-maccabees-4:7:3.summary: Those who “abandoned the holy covenant” under the king; general link to apostate leadership.

2-maccabees-4:10:0.summary: Lawless men persuade many to covenant with the nations, paralleling Jason turning countrymen to “the Greek manner of life”.

2-maccabees-4:14:0.summary: Priests treat the Lord’s table as “despised”, like priests “despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices”.

2-maccabees-4:17:0.summary: “God is not mocked… whatever a person sows, he will also reap”; general warning of consequences for impiety.
2-maccabees-4:17:0.note: Quoted wording here is paraphrased or comes from Hebrew-based translations, not the Saints text; compare the Saints readings.

2-maccabees-4:33:0.summary: “An anointing will be removed”; often linked to Onias’s murder, but the verse only reports his denunciation.

2-maccabees-4:33:1.summary: Speaks of a king acting falsely with a covenant; no clear link to Onias’s denunciation at Daphne.

2-maccabees-4:38:0.summary: “With the measure you use, it will be measured to you” fits Andronicus executed at the very place of his crime.

2-maccabees-4:38:1.summary: “Just as you acted, so it will be for you” matches the Lord rendering Andronicus “his deserved punishment”.

2-maccabees-5:2:1.summary: Heavenly “armies… upon white horses” parallel the armed horsemen seen racing through the air.

2-maccabees-5:11:1.summary: The king returns from campaign “his heart against the holy covenant”, matching Antiochus breaking camp in Egypt to attack Jerusalem.
2-maccabees-5:11:1.why: Daniel’s prophecy of this very event.

2-maccabees-5:19:0.summary: “The Sabbath was made for man, and not man for the Sabbath” mirrors the place chosen for the nation, not the nation for the place.
2-maccabees-5:19:0.why: Same reversal: institutions serve God’s people.

2-maccabees-5:20:0.summary: “For a short time I abandoned you… In a little anger” then mercy, matching what was abandoned in anger being restored when God was reconciled.

2-maccabees-5:21:1.summary: The tyrant says he will “ascend to heaven… be like the Most High”, like Antiochus’s haughty boast to sail the land and walk the sea.

2-maccabees-5:27:1.summary: The faithful wander “in deserts and mountains and caves”, matching Judas living in the wilderness and mountains.
2-maccabees-5:27:1.why: Hebrews likely recalls such Maccabean faithful.

2-maccabees-5:27:2.summary: “Judas, called Maccabeus” identifies the same person.

2-maccabees-5:27:3.summary: “Judas, called Maccabeus, arose in his place” names the same leader.

2-maccabees-6:1:0.summary: The king decrees all should “become one people”, parallel to compelling Jews to abandon ancestral laws.

2-maccabees-6:2:1.summary: Forces will “defile the sanctuary… and establish an abomination of desolation”, as the temple is defiled and named for Zeus.

2-maccabees-6:6:1.summary: Israel shall “keep the Sabbaths” as an everlasting covenant, contrasting with it being impossible to keep the Sabbath.

2-maccabees-6:7:0.summary: Monthly sacrifices offered “on the pagan altar” on the twenty-fifth parallel forced participation on the king’s monthly celebration.
2-maccabees-6:7:0.why: Parallel account of monthly pagan sacrifice.

2-maccabees-6:7:1.summary: Israelites dealt with “month after month” and pagan sacrifice on the twenty-fifth parallel the monthly compulsion.

2-maccabees-6:12:0.summary: “The Lord disciplines the one He loves” matches seeing punishments “for the discipline of our people, not their destruction”.

2-maccabees-6:12:1.summary: Scripture written “for our instruction” and encouragement; loosely parallel to urging readers of this book not to lose heart.

2-maccabees-6:14:saints-20261024-e6fa481.summary: God disciplines His sons while scourging enemies, giving others time, matching His different dealing with Israel and the nations.
2-maccabees-6:14:saints-20261024-e6fa481.why: Same theology of discipline versus delayed punishment.

2-maccabees-6:16:saints-20261024-6b7daf4.summary: “A merciful God; He will not forsake you” matches “He never withdraws His mercy… does not abandon His own people”.

2-maccabees-6:16:0.summary: God disciplines “for our benefit”, matching discipline through disaster that does not abandon His people.

2-maccabees-6:16:1.summary: “The Lord will not reject His people, nor abandon His inheritance” closely echoes “He does not abandon His own people”.

2-maccabees-6:18:0.summary: Many stood firm “against eating unclean things”, the same resistance Eleazar shows when forced to eat pork.

2-maccabees-6:19:1.summary: Others “were tortured, not accepting release”, fitting Eleazar going willingly to the torture frame.
2-maccabees-6:19:1.why: Hebrews likely recalls the Maccabean martyrs.

2-maccabees-6:26:0.summary: “A fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” echoes not escaping “the hands of the Almighty”.

2-maccabees-6:31:0.summary: Consider leaders’ “outcome” and imitate their faith; loosely parallels Eleazar’s death as an example.

2-maccabees-7:1:0.summary: “They chose to die so that they would not be defiled by foods”, the same martyrdom over forbidden food.

2-maccabees-7:1:1.summary: Those “tortured, not accepting release” for “a better resurrection” fits the seven brothers’ martyrdom.

2-maccabees-7:1:3.summary: Many resisted “eating unclean things” and chose death, paralleling the brothers forced to eat pork.

2-maccabees-7:2:0.summary: “We must obey God rather than human beings” matches readiness “to die rather than transgress our ancestral laws”.
2-maccabees-7:2:0.why: Same principle of obedience over coercion.

2-maccabees-7:6:1.summary: “The Lord will judge His people and be comforted concerning His slaves” is the Song of Moses line the brothers cite.

2-maccabees-7:9:1.summary: Those who did good rise “to a resurrection of life”, as the martyr expects to be raised to everlasting life.

2-maccabees-7:9:3.summary: The reward for those who “fall asleep in piety” shares the martyr’s resurrection hope within the same book.

2-maccabees-7:9:4.summary: Shares “release” and “everlasting” with the martyr’s words, but the thought differs.

2-maccabees-7:14:0.summary: Some arise “unto everlasting life, others unto reproach”, matching the martyr’s hope and the tyrant’s denial of resurrection to life.
2-maccabees-7:14:0.why: Daniel’s two destinies behind the martyr’s claim.

2-maccabees-7:14:2.summary: Paul’s “hope in God… resurrection” echoes looking “for the hopes given by God, to be raised again”.

2-maccabees-7:18:0.summary: “The Lord is righteous, for I embittered His mouth” matches “we suffer these things because of ourselves, having sinned”.
2-maccabees-7:18:0.why: Confession that suffering stems from sin.

2-maccabees-7:18:1.summary: Daniel confesses Jerusalem’s reproach is “because of our sins”, matching the martyr’s admission of sin.

2-maccabees-7:22:0.summary: God formed and supported the psalmist “from my mother’s womb”, as the mother says God, not she, formed her sons.
2-maccabees-7:22:0.why: God as author of life in the womb.

2-maccabees-7:22:2.summary: God clothed and threaded together the body, matching the mother’s denial that she arranged “the composition of each of you”.

2-maccabees-7:23:saints-20261024-4f7c195.summary: “I will put to death, and make alive” grounds the hope that the Creator gives “again both spirit and life”.
2-maccabees-7:23:saints-20261024-4f7c195.why: God’s power over death and life.

2-maccabees-7:23:1.summary: God brings “the breath of life” into dry bones, like the Creator giving again “spirit and life”.

2-maccabees-7:23:2.summary: God sends His Spirit and creatures “will be created”, linking creation and renewal as the mother does.

2-maccabees-7:23:3.summary: Razis calls on “the Master of life and spirit to give these back”, echoing the mother’s “gives you again both spirit and life”.
2-maccabees-7:23:3.why: Same resurrection language within the book.

2-maccabees-7:28:0.summary: “What is seen did not come into being from visible things” matches God making them “not from things that were”.

2-maccabees-7:28:3.summary: Heavens established “by the Lord’s word”; general creation theme without creation from nothing.

2-maccabees-7:28:4.summary: “Lift your eyes on high and see: Who displayed all these?” matches “look up at heaven and earth and see”.
2-maccabees-7:28:4.why: Same appeal to creation as evidence of God.

2-maccabees-7:33:0.summary: “In a little anger I turned My face… with everlasting mercy” matches being “angered briefly” then reconciled.

2-maccabees-7:33:1.summary: God’s anger is brief and “exultation comes toward morning”, matching His brief anger before reconciliation.

2-maccabees-7:36:saints-20261024-57e184a.summary: The righteous, “disciplined a little”, will receive great benefits and immortality, matching “short pain” leading to everlasting life.

2-maccabees-7:36:0.summary: “Momentary lightness of our affliction” produces “eternal” glory, matching “short pain” leading to everlasting life.

2-maccabees-7:36:1.summary: Present sufferings are not comparable to coming glory, paralleling short pain versus everlasting life.

2-maccabees-8:1:0.summary: “Judas, called Maccabeus” arises and his kin and supporters join him, paralleling the gathering of six thousand.

2-maccabees-8:3:1.summary: Blood that “speaks better than Abel”; both evoke blood crying out to God, but loosely.
2-maccabees-8:3:1.why: Image of blood calling to God.

2-maccabees-8:3:2.summary: Martyrs cry “avenge our blood”, matching the plea that God “listen to the blood crying out to Him”.

2-maccabees-8:4:0.summary: Mattathias sees “the blasphemies being committed in Judah”, the same blasphemies the prayer asks God to remember.

2-maccabees-8:8:0.summary: Lysias selects “Ptolemy son of Dorymenes”, the Ptolemy whom Philip asks for help.
2-maccabees-8:8:0.why: Identifies Ptolemy in the parallel account.

2-maccabees-8:16:0.summary: Judas sets out to strike the king’s force at Emmaus, the same campaign for which Maccabeus gathers his men.
2-maccabees-8:16:0.why: Parallel account of the Emmaus battle.

2-maccabees-8:16:1.summary: Judas says “Do not fear their multitude”, the same exhortation not to fear the multitude of nations.

2-maccabees-8:19:0.summary: God’s angel struck “a hundred and eighty-five thousand”, the Sennacherib deliverance Judas recounts.

2-maccabees-8:28:1.summary: The tithe is shared with the “orphan” and the “widow”, as the spoils are shared with widows and orphans.
2-maccabees-8:28:1.why: Torah basis for caring for the vulnerable.

2-maccabees-8:28:2.summary: Moses commands dividing “the spoils” between warriors and congregation, the precedent for sharing spoils.

2-maccabees-8:34:0.summary: A date in Artaxerxes’s kingdom has no link to Nicanor bringing merchants to sell Jews.

2-maccabees-8:34:1.summary: “The thrice-accursed man” is the same Nicanor described here with the same epithet.

2-maccabees-9:1:1.summary: The ruler came “to Persia with his force” and was cut down; a different account of Antiochus’s Persian disaster.
2-maccabees-9:1:1.why: Compare the book’s two Antiochus traditions.

2-maccabees-9:3:0.summary: The king hears reports, is shaken and falls ill, paralleling news reaching him of his forces’ defeat.
2-maccabees-9:3:0.why: Parallel account of Antiochus’s final illness.

2-maccabees-9:5:0.summary: Alcimus “was struck” and paralyzed; another enemy struck by sudden affliction, but different person.
2-maccabees-9:5:0.why: Another divine stroke on an enemy.

2-maccabees-9:5:1.summary: Herod is “struck” by God and “eaten by worms”, the same fate of an arrogant ruler as Antiochus.
2-maccabees-9:5:1.why: Same pattern of divine judgment on a proud king.

2-maccabees-9:8:1.summary: The tyrant would “ascend to heaven”, matching Antiochus’s arrogance “beyond human measure” and his fall.
2-maccabees-9:8:1.why: Hubris and downfall of the proud king.

2-maccabees-9:8:2.summary: Only God commands the sea, saying “your waves will be broken”, contrasting Antiochus thinking he could “command the waves”.
2-maccabees-9:8:2.why: Shows his boast claimed divine prerogative.

2-maccabees-9:9:0.summary: The martyr warns God “will torment you”, fulfilled in Antiochus’s agonizing decay.

2-maccabees-9:9:2.summary: “Their worm will not die” for transgressors made a spectacle, like worms swarming from the impious king.
2-maccabees-9:9:2.why: Image of worms as punishment of the wicked.

2-maccabees-9:12:saints-20261024-00d8404.summary: Tyre’s ruler said “I am a god… yet you are a human”, the claim Antiochus renounces: not to think oneself equal to God.

2-maccabees-9:28:2.summary: “The hour of his completion will come, and no one will help him”; loosely fits Antiochus’s lonely death, though locations differ.
2-maccabees-9:28:2.why: Prophetic end of the persecuting king.

2-maccabees-10:2:0.summary: Judas’s men cleanse the holy places and remove “the stones of defilement”, the same purge of foreign altars.
2-maccabees-10:2:0.why: Parallel narrative of the temple’s purification.

2-maccabees-10:6:saints-20261024-3f1b5f2.summary: Booths kept with “great gladness” for seven days plus an eighth-day observance, the model for the eight-day Booths-style celebration.
2-maccabees-10:6:saints-20261024-3f1b5f2.why: Shows the Booths pattern the festival imitated.

2-maccabees-10:6:1.summary: The law of the “Feast of Tents” for seven days with an eighth-day observance underlies celebrating “eight days in the manner of the Festival of Booths”.
2-maccabees-10:6:1.why: Legal basis for the festival format.

2-maccabees-10:7:0.summary: Simon’s men enter the citadel “with praise and palm branches… hymns”, the same victory celebration with palms and hymns.

2-maccabees-10:7:1.summary: Crowds take “branches of the palm trees” to welcome Jesus; shares festive palms only.
2-maccabees-10:7:1.why: Later use of palms in celebration.

2-maccabees-10:7:2.summary: The heavenly multitude holds “palm branches”; shares the palm-bearing worship image only.
2-maccabees-10:7:2.why: Palms as symbol of victory and worship.

2-maccabees-10:8:1.summary: “The feast of Dedication” is the annual festival decreed here for the entire Jewish nation.
2-maccabees-10:8:1.why: Shows the decreed feast still observed in Jesus’ day.

2-maccabees-10:24:0.summary: Timothy leads a strong force against Judas, the same enemy commander named here.
2-maccabees-10:24:0.why: Identifies Timothy in the parallel history.

2-maccabees-10:25:2.summary: Elders “put dust on their heads and girded themselves with sackcloth”, the same mourning gestures as Maccabeus’s men.
2-maccabees-10:25:2.why: Traditional gestures of supplication and lament.

2-maccabees-10:25:0.summary: Israel assembles “with fasting and in sackcloth”; shares only sackcloth as penitential practice.

2-maccabees-10:25:1.summary: Joshua and the elders “put dust on their heads” before the Lord after defeat, matching the supplication before battle.
2-maccabees-10:25:1.why: Same gesture of humbling before God in war.

2-maccabees-10:29:1.summary: A heavenly horseman with “golden armour” appears “leading them”, like the five riders with golden bridles leading the Jews.

2-maccabees-11:1:0.summary: Lysias assembles sixty thousand men and cavalry to make war, the parallel to Lysias’s campaign after his distress.
2-maccabees-11:1:0.why: Parallel account of Lysias’s first expedition.

2-maccabees-11:5:0.summary: The army encamps at “Beth-zur” and Judas meets them, the same site Lysias presses here.

2-maccabees-11:8:0.summary: Heavenly riders on horses with “golden bridles” appear “leading the Jews”, matching the golden-armoured horseman leading them.

2-maccabees-11:8:1.summary: Two men “in white garments” appear at the ascension; shares only the white-clad heavenly figure.

2-maccabees-11:8:2.summary: A heavenly warrior with drawn sword appears to Joshua before battle; general motif of divine champion.

2-maccabees-11:11:0.summary: About five thousand of “Lysias’s army fell” before Judas, parallel to the rout here though numbers differ.
2-maccabees-11:11:0.why: Compare figures in the parallel battle account.

2-maccabees-11:13:0.summary: “Lysias saw the rout” and the courage of Judas’s men, the same reflection on defeat recounted here.

2-maccabees-11:28:0.summary: John wishes that “all may go well with you” and “good health”, the same letter-greeting formula as “If you are well… in good health”.
2-maccabees-11:28:0.why: Shows a common ancient letter formula.

2-maccabees-12:17:0.summary: “The region of Tobiah” matches the Jews “called Toubiani” at Charax.
2-maccabees-12:17:0.why: Identifies the community Judas went to relieve.

2-maccabees-12:20:0.summary: Timothy’s army flees from “Maccabeus”, who strikes them a great blow; the parallel to Judas’s attack on Timothy.
2-maccabees-12:20:0.why: Parallel account of the campaign against Timothy.

2-maccabees-12:21:0.summary: “Carnaim” among strong cities matches “Carnion”, the hard-to-approach refuge Timothy used.

2-maccabees-12:29:0.summary: They cross the Jordan to the plain “opposite Beth-shan”, the city known as Scythopolis.

2-maccabees-12:31:0.summary: After the campaign they go up “to Mount Zion with gladness”, paralleling the return to Jerusalem.
2-maccabees-12:31:0.why: Parallel close of the Gilead campaign.

2-maccabees-12:31:2.summary: The law of counting “seven complete weeks” defines the “Festival of Weeks” they hurried to keep.

2-maccabees-12:31:3.summary: “The day of Pentecost” is the same Festival of Weeks, but it is only incidental to the source.
2-maccabees-12:31:3.why: Same festival in New Testament setting.

2-maccabees-12:40:1.summary: Achan’s forbidden spoil “hidden” in his tent caused defeat, like idol objects hidden under the fallen soldiers’ tunics.
2-maccabees-12:40:1.why: Classic precedent of hidden sin causing death in battle.

2-maccabees-12:41:1.summary: “Nothing is hidden that will not become manifest” echoes God “who makes hidden things manifest”.
2-maccabees-12:41:1.why: Same teaching on God exposing the hidden.

2-maccabees-12:43:0.summary: Paul argues from acts done “for the dead” to the resurrection, as Judas’s sin offering assumes the resurrection.
2-maccabees-12:43:0.why: Parallel reasoning from rites for the dead to resurrection.

2-maccabees-12:44:0.summary: “If the dead are not raised at all, why… baptized for them?” mirrors “if he did not expect those who had fallen to rise… foolish to pray for the dead”.
2-maccabees-12:44:0.why: Same argument form about resurrection and the dead.

2-maccabees-12:44:1.summary: Paul’s “if there is no resurrection of the dead” argument shares the resurrection premise but not prayer for the dead.

2-maccabees-12:45:0.summary: Those “sleeping” will “arise… unto everlasting life”, the hope behind the reward for those who “fall asleep in piety”.

2-maccabees-12:45:1.summary: The martyr trusts God will “raise us… unto everlasting renewal of life”, the same resurrection hope.
2-maccabees-12:45:1.why: Links Judas’s act to the martyrs’ faith.

2-maccabees-13:1:1.summary: Lysias makes the king’s son reign and calls him “Eupator”, the Antiochus Eupator who invades here.

2-maccabees-13:8:0.summary: The wicked “will fall into the hole he made”, the same fitting retribution as dying in ashes after sinning against the altar.

2-maccabees-13:8:1.summary: “All who take a sword will perish by a sword”; general principle of fitting retribution only.

2-maccabees-13:12:saints-20261024-a99b34.summary: Ezra proclaims a fast to seek God’s protection from enemies, and “He heard us”, like the three-day fast before battle.
2-maccabees-13:12:saints-20261024-a99b34.why: Model of fasting prayer before danger.

2-maccabees-14:12:0.summary: The king sends a commander with “the ungodly Alcimus”; a related dispatch, but of Bacchides, not Nicanor.
2-maccabees-14:12:0.why: Context of Demetrius’s campaigns with Alcimus.

2-maccabees-14:13:1.summary: Shares Judas and Alcimus as persons, describing Alcimus’s evil rather than Nicanor’s orders.

2-maccabees-14:18:0.summary: Nicanor sends to Judas “with peaceful words”, paralleling his reluctance to decide matters by bloodshed.
2-maccabees-14:18:0.why: Parallel account with a harsher view of Nicanor’s motives.

2-maccabees-14:42:0.summary: Saul falls on his sword “lest these uncircumcised men… mock me”, like Razis choosing death over outrage.
2-maccabees-14:42:0.why: Precedent for death to avoid enemy abuse.

2-maccabees-14:46:0.summary: The Creator “gives you again both spirit and life”, echoed in Razis calling on the Master of life and spirit “to give these back”.
2-maccabees-14:46:0.why: Shared resurrection hope in bodily restoration.

2-maccabees-15:3:0.summary: “The thrice-accursed Nicanor” identifies the “thrice-accursed man” of this verse.
2-maccabees-15:3:0.why: Identifies the speaker by the same epithet.

2-maccabees-15:3:1.summary: A date in Artaxerxes’s kingdom (thirteenth of Adar) has no link to Nicanor’s question about the Sabbath.

2-maccabees-15:4:0.summary: The commandment “Remember the Sabbath day” is the command the Jews cite from the Sovereign in heaven.
2-maccabees-15:4:0.why: Source of the Sabbath command invoked.

2-maccabees-15:9:0.summary: Scripture written “for our instruction” gives “encouragement”, as Judas encourages his men “from the law and the prophets”.
2-maccabees-15:9:0.why: Same use of Scripture to strengthen endurance.

2-maccabees-15:22:0.summary: A prayer for vengeance on Nicanor’s army; related prayer before battle but lacks the Sennacherib precedent.

2-maccabees-15:22:3.summary: An angel “killed one hundred eighty-five thousand from the Assyrians’ camp”, the very event Judas recalls.
2-maccabees-15:22:3.why: Original account of the deliverance cited.

2-maccabees-15:32:0.summary: They “cut off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had stretched out arrogantly” and displayed them.

2-maccabees-15:35:1.summary: David brings the enemy champion’s head to Jerusalem, like Judas hanging Nicanor’s head as a sign of victory.
2-maccabees-15:35:1.why: Precedent for displaying a defeated foe’s head.

2-maccabees-15:36:1.summary: Jews observe “the fourteenth of Adar” as a festive day, the “Mordecai’s day” that Nicanor’s Day precedes.
2-maccabees-15:36:1.why: Explains the reference to Mordecai’s day.

2-maccabees-15:36:2.summary: Establishing “the fourteenth and fifteenth of Adar” as festive days identifies Mordecai’s day.

2-maccabees-15:36:3.summary: “The twelfth month, on the thirteenth day… which is Adar” is the same date set for Nicanor’s Day.
